questions.question: A coin has one head and one tail. What can you say about the chance of getting heads?
questions.explain: A coin has two equal sides, so heads and tails have the same chance. A common trap is thinking one side is bigger or better just because you like it.

questions.question: You flip a coin and get heads. You flip again and get heads. You flip a third time. What is the chance of heads?
questions.explain: Every flip is its own new chance, the same as before. A common trap is thinking that after two heads, tails becomes due or heads becomes tired.

questions.question: A bag has 3 red balls and 3 blue balls. You pick one. What is the chance of red?
questions.explain: With 3 red and 3 blue, the numbers are equal, so red and blue have the same chance. A common trap is thinking the order you name them or the total number changes the chance.

questions.question: Sam flips a coin 6 times. He gets 5 heads and 1 tail. He says, 'The next flip MUST be tails because it is due.' Is he right?
options: No, each flip is the same
questions.explain: Each coin flip is its own new chance, so the chance stays the same every time. A common trap is thinking that after many heads, tails becomes overdue or owed.

questions.question: Lily spins a two-colour spinner (half red, half blue) 20 times. She gets 14 red and 6 blue. Is the spinner broken?
options: Yes, red is winning too many
questions.explain: A fair spinner can give more of one colour in a short number of spins, and that is still a fair result. A common trap is thinking 20 spins must give exactly 10 and 10.

questions.question: You and your friend each flip a coin once. You get heads. What is the chance your friend gets tails?
questions.explain: Your flip and your friend's flip are separate, so the chance for each is the same. A common trap is thinking that because you got heads, your friend is owed a tails.

questions.question: A bag has 4 stickers: 2 cats, 2 dogs. You pick one, look, and put it back. You pick again. What is the chance of a cat?
options: The same as the first pick
questions.explain: Because you put the sticker back, the bag is the same for the second pick, so the chance is the same. A common trap is thinking that seeing one sticker changes what is left in the bag.

questions.question: Tom flips a coin 10 times and gets 8 heads, 2 tails. He says, 'I must keep flipping until I get 5 tails, because a fair coin means exactly half.' What is the best answer?
options: The next one must be tails
He is right, the coin is odd
He should only count the tails
questions.explain: A fair coin can give 8 heads and 2 tails in 10 flips, and that is a normal fair result. A common trap is thinking fair means the results must be exactly half and half.

questions.question: A jar has 5 red and 5 blue marbles. You pull one, look, and put it back. You do this 12 times and get 9 red, 3 blue. Your friend says, 'Red must stop now.' What do you say?
options: Red is winning, so it stops
questions.explain: In 12 pulls, getting 9 and 3 is a fair, normal mix for equal numbers of marbles. A common trap is thinking that after more reds, red must stop or that you need exactly 6 and 6.

questions.question: Anna flips a coin 4 times: H, H, H, H. She says, 'The 5th flip MUST be tails because a fair coin has to balance out.' What is the mistake?
options: Each flip is a new chance
The coin ran out of heads
questions.explain: Each flip is a new, independent chance, so four heads do not owe the next flip a tail. A common trap is thinking a fair coin has to balance out in a short stretch of flips.

questions.question: A spinner is half orange and half purple. You give it one spin. What is the chance of landing on orange?
questions.explain: The two halves are the same size, so orange and purple have an even chance. A spinner does not take turns or follow an order.

questions.question: At a soccer game the ref tosses a coin. Your team gets the ball if it lands tails. What is the chance of tails?
questions.explain: A coin has one head and one tail, so tails has the same chance as heads. Even chance does not mean the sides take turns.

questions.question: A bag holds 5 green cubes and 5 yellow cubes. You pick one without looking. Which is true?
questions.explain: There are just as many green cubes as yellow cubes, so each colour has an even chance. Even chance does not promise an exact split.

questions.question: Maya and Ben flip a coin to see who plays first. Maya picks heads. Is this fair?
options: No, tails is due to win
questions.explain: Heads and tails have the same chance, so the flip is fair for both kids. It stays fair even when one side wins a few times in a row.

questions.question: Noah spins a spinner that is half blue and half white. In 8 spins he gets blue 6 times. He says white must come next because it is due. What is the mistake?
options: Blue is the one that is due.
questions.explain: Each spin is a fresh 50-50, and the spinner cannot remember the 6 blues. Colours do not owe each other turns.

questions.question: A bag has 4 red marbles and 1 blue marble. Nina wants red and blue to have an even chance. How many blue marbles should she add?
questions.explain: Adding 3 blue gives 4 red and 4 blue, so the colours are equally likely. Adding 4 forgets the 1 blue marble that is already in the bag.

questions.question: Ben's bag has 3 black counters and 5 white counters. He puts in 2 more black counters. Which is true now?
options: Black is due to come up
questions.explain: 3 black and 2 more make 5 black, and there are 5 white, so the chance is 50-50. Same numbers means an even chance, not a promise about what comes out.

questions.question: Tia and Raj want a fair way to pick who bats first. Tia says flip a coin. Raj says spin a spinner with 3 red parts and 1 yellow part. Whose way gives an even chance?
questions.explain: A coin has two equal sides, so heads and tails are 50-50. Raj's spinner has more red parts than yellow, so red is more likely and the chance is not even.
